policy_title: Extend and Increase Windfall Tax on Oil and Gas Giants
stated: Labour will extend the sunset clause of the Energy Profits Levy until the end of the next parliament and increase the levy rate by three percentage points. They will also remove 'unjustifiably generous' investment allowances and retain the Energy Security Investment Mechanism, aiming to fund clean energy investments from company profits rather than ingenuity or investment.

source.quote: To support investment in this plan, Labour will close the loopholes in the windfall tax on oil and gas companies. Companies have benefitted from enormous profits not because of their ingenuity or investment, but because of an energy shock which raised prices for British families. Labour will therefore extend the sunset clause in the Energy Profits Levy until the end of the next parliament. We will also increase the rate of the levy by three percentage points, as well as removing the unjustifiably generous investment allowances. Labour will also retain the Energy Security Investment Mechanism.

bearing_set.reason: Removing investment allowances reduces incentive for new fossil-fuel extraction, and revenues are directed to clean-energy investment — both channels directly affect the UK's emissions trajectory.

Energy bills are a core cost-of-living indicator; the levy's effect on domestic oil/gas investment (and hence supply/security) and the stated use of proceeds to fund clean energy create a non-negligible projected path to consumer energy costs.

Stripping investment allowances cuts the fiscal incentive for new upstream oil-and-gas capex; reduced North Sea investment has a concrete, documented mechanism for job losses in the sector, directly moving the employment-rate and job-security indicators for tens of thousands of workers.
Extending and increasing the levy raises material additional tax revenue from oil and gas profits, directly improving the funded/borrowed balance of public spending.

Curtailing investment allowances risks deterring capital expenditure in the North Sea, a mechanism flagged by industry bodies (OEUK) and OBR analysis; reduced upstream investment would affect UK energy sector output, employment, and productivity — a non-negligible cross-outcome cost on living standards and economic opportunity.

membership_note: Three genuine bearings: a fiscal improvement (O12), an environmental lever via reduced fossil-fuel investment incentives and clean-energy funding (O6), and a prospective investment-deterrence risk (O13). Corporate incidence means O11 (household tax burden) does not apply directly; global energy pricing limits any O2 pass-through mechanism; O4 job-security effects are real but subsumed under the O13 investment/output mechanism at sector level.
